newsitem.title: USA: U.S Sen. Lugar seeks to reform forex rules next yr.
newsitem.headline: U.S Sen. Lugar seeks to reform forex rules next yr.

text.p: U.S. Senator Richard Lugar said on Monday he expects to propose reforming problematic laws governing foreign exchange trading next year.
Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee, said such a reform would not be part of a bill he is introducing this week to amend the Commodity Exchange Act.
"There's not agreement within the government," on the foreign exchange trading issue, Lugar said in an interview Monday on CNBC.
Under a 1974 amendment to the Commodity Exchange Act, interbank forex trading is not regulated like futures trading.
But ambiguities have arisen concerning the scope of the amendment and the Supreme Court will hear a case on the issue next term.
Lugar had asked the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Department of the Treasury to hammer out a compromise on the amendment by September but the agencies have not reached agreement yet.
"We have indicated that we are going to touch these areas in essence when we come to the actual legislation next year, Lugar said. "Clearly we hope there will be better agreement, less disarray."
"We've given the parties some time to think about it through the Christmas vacation," Lugar said. "But when we come back in January, we need to hear about it."
Lugar said even the reform proposals he is introducing this week will not be passed in the current legislative session, but will set the stage for action next year.
"Everybody anticipates that we are going to offer constructive legislation and that's why we're doing that," Lugar said. "So there are no surprises and people have a chance to massage the language."

The bill to be introduced this week will include several changes requested by U.S. futures exchanges, including allowing the exchanges to begin trading in new contracts far more quickly than permitted under current law.
The bill would also mandate that the CFTC use a cost-benefit analysis before imposing new regulations and free the exchanges from a requirement to deploy high-tech trade auditing systems.
The bill would also give the CFTC new jurisdiction over foreign futures contracts that can be delivered on in the United States.
